title: Quiet Yoga Seat
on_slide_text: Sage Valmiki sits alone on a soft seat of kusha grass. He closes his eyes and thinks deeply about Rama through yoga. Narada has left for the sky after telling Rama's brief tale. Now in quiet stillness, a full new story begins to rise.
rationale: Opens on the hook of Valmiki alone in yoga, from which the whole tale rises.

title: Twenty Four Thousand Verses
on_slide_text: After Rama receives the kingdom of Ayodhya, Valmiki writes his whole life in sweet verses. The poem holds twenty four thousand verses in five hundred parts and seven books. Each word is full of deep sense. With clear yogic sight he joins what happened with what will come.
rationale: Establishes the completed Ramayana with its vast size and yogic scope.

title: Who Will Sing First
on_slide_text: The great poem is now complete and ready. Valmiki looks around his quiet hut and thinks hard. Who will sing this holy tale first before learned groups. The story is too big for one voice alone. It needs fresh young throats to carry it far.
rationale: Shows Valmiki searching for first singers, creating the need for Kush and Lav.

title: Two Boys Touch Feet
on_slide_text: Two bright boys enter in simple ascetic dress and touch Valmiki's feet. They are Kush and Lav, princes who live in the hut and love right action. Their voices ring sweet and clear. They learn quick, remember fast, and already know the holy Vedas well.
rationale: Introduces Kush and Lav arriving and their bright fitness to learn.

title: Eyes To Judge Right
on_slide_text: Before giving the sweet story, Valmiki first opens their inner eye. He teaches Kush and Lav how to find true sense in the Vedas. He shows how to weigh right and wrong in every line. Only clear thought can hold a holy tale right.
rationale: Covers Valmiki first teaching Vedic sense before handing the story.

title: Sense Before Story
question: Why did Valmiki teach Kush and Lav how to judge sense before giving the sweet Rama tale?
answer: Because a sweet voice alone only entertains. Valmiki knew meaning must come first. He gave them clear eyes to judge right, then gave the lamp of story. Singing is art, but living the sense is true learning.
on_slide_text: Why teach sense before story to Kush and Lav? Because a sweet tale without clear thought is only fun, not guide. Valmiki gave first the eye to judge, then the lamp of tale. This week pause before you share a story and teach one child how to find its right sense.
rationale: Pauses to draw the first reflection on sense before story.

title: Tale Learned By Heart
on_slide_text: Then Valmiki teaches the boys the whole Ramayana by heart. The tale holds Sita's pure life and the fall of Ravana. Kush and Lav learn each verse with love and care. They keep the holy words safe in strong young memory.
rationale: Covers entrusting of the whole Ramayana centered on Sita and Ravana's fall.

title: Seven Notes With Veena
on_slide_text: Kush and Lav shine bright like young Gandharvas in song and dance. They learn tune steps called Sthana and Murchhana with care. They sing in three speeds and seven clear notes with the veena. Their song can show love, grief, fun, anger, fear, and brave hearts.
rationale: Details the musical mastery that makes the tale singable and felt.

title: Singing Before Good Folk
on_slide_text: With full love the two princes learn the whole holy tale by heart. They keep their minds calm and fixed on each word. Then they go to sing before ascetics, Brahmanas, and good folk. They sing just as Valmiki taught, with no change.
rationale: Moves the singers from hut to public assemblies exactly as taught.

title: Small Voices Carry Far
question: Why did Valmiki not carry his great tale to Ayodhya himself, but send two small boys to sing it?
answer: Because kings seldom hear old sages with open hearts. They hear pure children. Kush and Lav are like Rama's own face in a clear mirror. When Valmiki stepped back, the tale grew bigger than him and could live in young throats for all time.
on_slide_text: Why send children, not go himself with the great tale? Because power often guards a sage but only hears a pure young voice. Kush and Lav mirror Rama to himself. This week let a young voice speak one of your ideas, and you sit back and just listen well.
rationale: Reflects on why children, not the author, carry the tale to power.

title: Well Done Well Done
on_slide_text: One day Kush and Lav sing in a large group of pure ascetics. Holy marks shine bright on their young limbs. Hearing them, the sages weep with joy and cry well done, well done. They say the old tale feels alive, as if we see it with our own eyes now.
rationale: Shows the first great singing where sages weep that past feels present.

title: One High Sweet Tune
on_slide_text: Both brothers sing as one in a high sweet tune. Their pure notes like Shadja fill the still air. The sound holds every heart in the group. Even proud sages strong in hard penance never tire of praising their song again and again.
rationale: Holds on united high singing that never tires praise.

title: Tears That Remember
question: Why did hard ascetics weep with tears, when the tale was bound in seven notes and strong feelings?
answer: Because the mind forgets dry facts, but the heart keeps tears. Valmiki wrapped truth in sweet song and strong feelings, so ears could see. When learning melts into feeling, it stays deep inside. Calm hearts still feel, but their feelings are clean and bright.
on_slide_text: Why bind old history in music that brings tears? Because dry facts slip from mind, but felt song stays in heart. Valmiki made listeners see, not just hear. This week turn one dry rule at home into a small song or play, and watch what hearts truly keep.
rationale: Draws the memory science that feeling makes history stay.

title: Pots And Bark Robes
on_slide_text: Pleased sages give simple gifts from kind hearts. One gives a water pot, one gives a bark cloth robe. One gives a soft black deer skin for sitting. One gives a holy thread, and one gives a small clay pot for holy use.
rationale: Begins the gift flow of useful ascetic things, not gold.

title: Axe Firewood And Blessings
on_slide_text: More gifts keep coming for the young singers. One gives a grass belt, one a soft mat to sit on. One gives a small cloth, one an axe for wood work. One gives red cloth and string for hair, one fire sticks and a fig wood seat, with blessings for long life.
rationale: Completes the gift list and blessings for long life.

title: Giving That Helps Work
question: Why did wise sages give no gold coins, but plain things like a pot, an axe, and firewood?
answer: Because true giving helps life, not show. The sages had no gold, but they knew need. A pot gives water, an axe helps work, a seat steadies prayer. Their best gift was a blessing that the song would feed new poets for all time to come.
on_slide_text: Why give a pot and axe, not gold coins? Because kind giving feeds practice, not pride. A pot cools thirst, an axe aids work, a seat holds prayer. This week give a young talent not just praise, but a real tool, time, or friend that keeps their work alive.
rationale: Reflects on true giving as sustaining practice.

title: Song For Future Poets
on_slide_text: All truth speaking sages bless the boys with warm words. They say your sweet song delights ear and heart and brings long life. You have sung the holy poem well to its end. This same song will give new ideas to poets yet to be born.
rationale: Records the blessing that the poem will seed future poets.

title: Singers In Market Street
on_slide_text: Honoured in many places, the two singers walk one day in Ayodhya street. Stalls stand in bright rows on both sides of the road. People stop to look at the twin boys with veenas in hand. Their sweet fame has now reached the king's own city.
rationale: Shifts the scene to Ayodhya street where fame reaches the city.

title: Called To King's House
on_slide_text: Shri Ram, Bharata's elder brother, sees the boys in the city. He calls the worthy singers to his house with love. The brave king greets them with full honour and kind care. Two young ascetics now stand before the great king of Ayodhya.
rationale: Brings the singers before Shri Ram who welcomes them with honour.

slide_label: Slide20 - Open Your Ears And Hearts
title: Open Your Ears And Hearts
speaker: Shri Ram
on_slide_text: Shri Ram sits on a bright gold throne with his brothers and wise guides near. He looks at the modest handsome boys and speaks. Lakshmana, Bharata, Shatrughna, hear this tale of deep sense. These bright youths sing with god given voice, so open your ears and hearts.
rationale: Seats the court to listen at Rama's order to the divine song.

title: Hair Stands On End
on_slide_text: At Rama's word Kush and Lav lift their clear sweet voices high. Their song rings like the soft strings of a veena. The hair of hearers stands up and hearts open wide with joy. Every ear in the full court is caught and held by that pure sound.
rationale: Captures the singing effect that thrills ears and hearts.

title: Royal Marks Shine Through
speaker: Shri Ram
on_slide_text: Shri Ram smiles and speaks to the full court with warm praise. These boys look like hard ascetics, yet royal signs shine on them. This tale spreads my fame and holds great worth. Hear it with care, for it shows the right path for all.
rationale: Voices Rama seeing royalty under ascetic dress and worth of the tale.

slide_label: Slide23 - From Hut To Bright Court
title: From Hut To Bright Court
on_slide_text: At his order they sing in the pure old Marga style. Shri Ram sits in the midst and sinks deep into the music. He wishes his life tale to live for all ages to come. So Valmiki's song travels from quiet hut to the king's bright court.
rationale: Closes the story arc as hut song reaches court in Marga style.

title: The King Who Listened
question: Why should a king hear his own tale, is that pride?
answer: Because hearing makes a doer a seer. On the throne Rama turned king into listener. He saw royal worth under plain dress, not outer show. Keeping the tale alive guides future people. Only one who truly listens can rule with care.
on_slide_text: Why should a king hear his own tale, is that pride? No, it is clear self seeing. Rama left the throne in heart to listen and learn. He looked past plain dress to true worth. This week hear your own story from a trusted friend for five still minutes, and ask what it teaches.
rationale: Ends on the sharpest insight that listening makes one worthy to rule.
